stances.claim: The Manila Prince Hotel was not part of the national 'economy and patrimony' warranting constitutional Filipino preference, and the majority subverted the essence of public bidding by giving the award to a losing Filipino bidder who merely equaled — not bettered — the Malaysian offer.
stances.rhetorical_move: dissent-resurrection: re-asserting CJ's own minority view as the legally correct position against the majority's holding

stances.claim: Mining industry underperformance is directly traceable to 'festering policy volatility' — the SC reversing itself (8-5 to 10-4) on the Mining Law in the same year — proving that credible, stable long-term policy is a prerequisite for venture capital in gestation-heavy extractive industries.
stances.rhetorical_move: policy-consequence attribution: linking doctrinal instability directly to investor lukewarmness

stances.claim: The Charter's economic provisions can be construed more liberally to attract investment without amendment, as demonstrated by Gamboa (limiting the 40% foreign ownership cap to voting shares) and PSALM (allowing dam-collected water to be used commercially by a Korean firm).
stances.rhetorical_move: interpretive-flexibility argument: liberal reading as an investment-friendly alternative to constitutional amendment

notable_anecdotes: Justice Scalia declining CJ Panganiban's invitation to the 2006 Global Forum, saying 'you do not really want me there' because he swore to defend only the US Constitution as originally intended and not international law — then directing CJ to 'my friend next door, Justice Kennedy,' who agreed to speak via video teleconference: a cameo that dramatizes the originalism vs internationalism divide at the highest judicial level.

CJ Panganiban writing the December 1, 2004 reversal in La Bugal — upholding the very Mining Law his own Court had struck down 11 months earlier — while Justice Carpio, who led the dissenters in that reversal, now leads a reconstituted Court being asked to revisit the same issues: a doctrinal pendulum CJ cites as the root cause of mining industry stagnation.

Justice Azcuna as one of the 10 holders of the 'Chief Justice Panganiban Professorial Chair on Liberty and Prosperity' — a quiet self-referential institutional disclosure that situates the lecture within CJ Panganiban's own endowed academic legacy.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reports on Justice Azcuna's lecture at the Ateneo Law School dissecting four controversial SC decisions on the economic provisions of the Constitution. First, Manila Prince Hotel vs GSIS (1997): the SC directed the award of Manila Hotel to a losing Filipino bidder who equaled a Malaysian competitor's higher bid, citing the Filipino-preference clause -- CJ Panganiban dissented, arguing the hotel was not part of national patrimony and that public bidding was subverted when the 'ballgame is over.' Second, La Bugal-B'laan vs Ramos: the SC struck down the Mining Law 8-5 in January 2004, then reversed itself 10-4 in December 2004 -- CJ wrote the reversal upholding the FTAA on condition that ultimate control remained with the President -- but this 'festering policy volatility' has kept the mining industry from growing. Third, Gamboa vs Teves (2011): the 40% foreign ownership cap in public utilities applies only to voting shares. Fourth, PSALM (2012): river water is a national resource, but once appropriated and collected in a dam it becomes private and usable by a Korean firm for electricity generation. CJ closes with a Scalia-Kennedy anecdote on originalism vs international-law interpretation, framing it as the meta-debate underlying all four decisions.
